title: Is Artificial Intelligence undermining Freedom of Information?
content:
Guest post by Ben Worthy, David Cuillier, Sheeley Kimball and Suzanne Piotrowski

There is growing concern that Artificial Intelligence is undermining Freedom of Information laws, and that ‘bots’ can be used to ‘flood’ or overwhelm public bodies with requests. In 2023 Wired magazine reported widespread worries that AI bots could flood FOIA officers working in elections in the US, claiming that ‘Election Workers Are Drowning in Records Requests. AI Chatbots Could Make It Worse’. In 2025, the Australian Attorney General proposed a series of restrictions to the Australian Federal FOI law, arguing that ‘technology [is] enabling large volumes of vexatious, abusive and frivolous requests—tying up resources, costing taxpayers money and delaying genuine requests’, and citing claims of ‘FOI bombing’ of particular agencies. The UK government also recently floated the possibility of altering cost limits, again with a hint that AI was driving increased requests. In June 2026 the Scottish Information Commissioner spoke of the ‘potential challenges posed by high‑volumes of AI‑generated requests’ meaning ‘excessive or automated submissions can place considerable strain on organisational resources’.

title: This FixMyStreet report really got things changed
content:
You might think that the impact of one FixMyStreet report is pretty simple: report a pothole, and it gets filled in. Report graffiti, it gets removed. Good results, but perhaps limited in scope.

Then again, just sometimes, a report goes further. It depends on a lot of things, prime among them the council’s willingness to listen to their residents and understand when there is a need to make change.

This particular story began last June with a report on Dogdyke Road in Lincolnshire. “I live on a park home site”, the report-maker began, explaining that most of his fellow residents were older, and many could not drive.

“We have a bus route [and] there is a bus shelter, but […] the bus cannot use this. So the passengers waiting for the bus towards Lincoln have to walk on the grass verge when the bus emerges. You can appreciate the grass is sometimes wet and slippery; also the grass verge is not the same level when the bus stops to pick up the passengers.”

title: Bioregional use the Scorecards framework to guide councils on their climate action
content:
The Council Climate Action Scorecards were originally conceived as a way for the public to understand how well the UK’s councils were doing on decarbonisation. It was immediately obvious that they were an invaluable tool for councils themselves, too; and we’ve seen many instances of campaign groups using Scorecards evidence to underpin their lobbying. But we recently heard, for the first time, of a novel usage: a purpose-led sustainability consultancy using the Scorecards to structure their guidance.

Bioregional supports organisations of all kinds on their path to net zero. Having heard that they use the Council Climate Action Scorecards in their work with local authorities, we were keen to chat with Nina Wallace, their Senior Sustainability Consultant, to find out more.

First of all, how does Bioregional’s consultancy intersect with the work councils are already doing to reach their net zero targets?

title: AI-authored contributions to our codebases
content:
mySociety has had a longstanding mission to help avoid the reinvention of the wheel in civic tech. That’s why most of our code is open source, and that’s what has allowed people to run instances of sites like FixMyStreet, WhatDoTheyKnow and TheyWorkForYou in their own jurisdictions, without having to write code or manage challenges, such as those we mentioned in our previous post, themselves.

So perhaps, rather than hearing about your whole new website, we’d prefer to see you submit some AI-authored code to our existing open source codebases?

title: So you’ve vibe coded a website and you’d like us to take a look
content:
AI tools that allow people without coding skills to spin up a website are now commonplace, and this has resulted in a rapid rise in people getting in touch with us here at mySociety. These days, a large number of the emails we’re receiving begin something like: “Hey, I’ve created this website…”

While it’s not always explicitly mentioned, it’s pretty clear the vast majority of these sites have been vibe coded — that is, written entirely by AI, most likely based only on descriptions of the intended output, and almost always without any human review or even understanding of the underlying code.

We love to hear from the civic tech community, and of course we have a keen interest in technology that makes democracy more accessible. As AI is lowering the bar to folk making a tool they’ve imagined into a reality, new projects are launching thick and fast. We’d be foolish to ignore that.

But that said, we are getting a lot of emails.

title: Developed for the public sector and kept public: explaining open source licensing
content:
We’ve copied this post from the blog of mySociety’s commercial subsidiary SocietyWorks. It’s part 2 in their Responsible Tech series, in which they explore open source technology and data privacy, security, and sovereignty. In this update, Chloe Carrington Dunn explains what open source licensing is, how to spot it and what public sector decision-makers need to know about it.

— 

The first post in this series explored the benefits of open and reusable source code. Angela Dixon, our Managing Director, made the case that “if it is the product of public spend, then it should be built to be reused and shared” and busted some of the myths around open source being more vulnerable to maleficent actors or less secure. 

If you didn’t read that first post, the tl;dr was this: publishing open source code can reduce risk, prevent vendor lock-in, and means the benefits of the code can be shared among other public sector entities. 

But not everyone understands what open source means and how to recognise when something is open source. In this blog post, I’ll clear up when open source code is used, what it means to be open, and what this means for the public sector.

title: Digital Democracy Edinburgh: call for proposals and registration now open
content:
Digital Democracy Edinburgh, presented by TICTeC, is an international two-day conference that will take place in Scotland’s capital city on 11 & 12 March 2027.

Policymakers, researchers, civic tech practitioners, public servants, and democratic innovators will come together to explore democratic futures and how digital tools can help make democratic institutions around the world more effective, inclusive and resilient.

We’re delighted to share that registration for the conference is now open, allowing both in-person and online access.

We’ve also just opened up a call for session/presentation proposals, which invites individuals, and groups of contributors, to submit their ideas for the conference proceedings. Read on to learn what we’re looking for in proposals.

Digital Democracy Edinburgh is a collaboration between the Scottish Government, the University of Edinburgh Futures Institute, mySociety, and the AI for Collective Intelligence (AI4CI) Hub.

Digital Democracy Edinburgh is made possible with additional generous support from the Evens Foundation, RadicalxChange and Delib.

title: From volunteer to town councillor, with the Council Climate Action Scorecards
content:
Kiran Crawford volunteered for the Council Climate Action Scorecards — and now he’s a town councillor, using everything the Scorecards taught him about local authorities’ powers to take climate action.

Kiran was elected as a Green councillor for Royal Leamington Spa Town council in July 2026. Prior to that, as a longtime volunteer with Climate Emergency UK, he helped make the Scorecards a reality.

“I originally volunteered for the first iteration of the Scorecards back in 2021, after hearing about them from a friend who had also signed up as a volunteer.

“Having been involved in some climate campaigning before, I was looking for more ways to support good policy. The Scorecards sounded like a great way to find out how good councils’ plans were, and I thought they could be really helpful tool in campaigning for action, so I signed up to help with the assessments.

“I found the process really interesting, and learnt a lot about what powers councils have around climate. Given how useful I could see the Scorecards would be, I then volunteered as a media amplifier to help get the launch out to the press, so that they could reach as many people as possible.

title: TICTeC Presents: Digital Democracy Edinburgh (11 & 12 March 2027)
content:
Digital Democracy Edinburgh will take place on 11 & 12 March 2027 in Edinburgh, Scotland. 

Save the date to join us for two days of exploring how digital tools can help make democratic systems more effective, inclusive and participatory.

How can we practically use technology to improve democratic decision-making and resilience?

This is the core question of this event, which we will answer by bringing together a global audience of practitioners and experts from civic tech, democratic innovation, and local and national governments.

Through the conference, we will explore how high-quality, deliberative, participation can be enhanced through digital technology, in democracies around the world. We will explore the use of technology to make collective decisions, solve shared problems, and govern ourselves effectively.

This means bringing together expertise and cutting-edge findings to support groups contributing to difficult decisions around the world – including findings about the uses of AI technologies which the public can trust.

title: They work for you (and we do too)
content:
We run TheyWorkForYou to make UK politics more accessible and accountable.

Here’s what we’ve been doing recently to make that happen.

Our alerts service will send you an email whenever your chosen keyword or phrase is mentioned in Parliament; or you can follow any MP or other representative to receive an email when they speak or vote.

So far in 2026, we’ve sent 2.2 million email alerts and our users have created almost 2,000 new keyword alerts through our new and improved alerts management system.

This service helps people understand what their representatives (across all of the UK’s Parliaments) are saying and doing, and also provides an essential service in providing free parliamentary monitoring to civic groups and organisations who can now have as much access to this intel as those with big pockets.

This doesn’t happen by itself: every day our team pulls together the transcripts from the UK’s Parliaments, fixing formatting issues and broken files to get these loaded into the site and our alerts.

If you don’t have alerts set up, what are you waiting for? You can do it now at TheyWorkForYou.com.
